question: The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act has been heavily criticised for the legal constraints it places on free scientific research. As a result, there is a lack of investment in AI in the EU, and qualified AI personnel are leaving in droves, particularly to the United States. 1.
Is the Commission willing to review AI regulations to provide more flexibility for European research?
In view of the massive AI investment programmes being pursued by the US and China, how will the Commission make sure the EU once again becomes a key, indispensable technology player?
Given the significant amounts of stable and affordable energy needed to develop AI infrastructure, does the Commission intend to massively promote the deployment of nuclear energy in Europe?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) The AI Act1 does not apply to AI systems or models developed and used exclusively for scientific research and development2, nor to AI research, testing or development activities before they are placed on the market or put into service3. The Commission is developing guidelines clarifying the scope of the exclusion.
While the AI Omnibus recently entered into force4, the Digital Omnibus5 further aims to support scientific research and responsible AI development in the EU.

The Commission considers AI as a strategic area for the EU’s competitiveness and technological sovereignty and launched several initiatives for the development of frontier AI models and systems as strategic assets for the EU and to support AI Science and the applications of AI in scientific domains6.

The Commission continues to support the development and uptake of AI through EU-level actions on research, innovation, digital infrastructure and skills. The Commission recognises that AI infrastructure requires secure and affordable electricity and supports all zero- and low-carbon solutions that can help meet this need, including nuclear7, as reflected in the Small Modular Reactors Strategy8.

For Member States choosing nuclear, the Commission’s role is to support the conditions under which it can contribute to common European objectives, notably decarbonisation, competitiveness and security of supply. EU AI policy also prioritises energy-efficient, sustainable data centres and their integration into the energy system9.

Alongside clear incentives for the data centre sector to transition to a clean energy system, the proposal for the Cloud and AI Development Act10 also promotes data centres’ on-site generation and storage of clean energy.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng. 2 Article 2(6) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. 3 Article 2(8) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. ‘Such activities shall be conducted in accordance with applicable

Union law. Testing in real world conditions shall not be covered by that exclusion’. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025PC0836. 5 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/digital-omnibus-regulation-proposal. 6 European Frontier AI Initiative, European Strategy for AI in Science, and the Resource for AI Science in Europe (RAISE). 7 https://energy.ec.europa.
